Vulkan drivers are not guaranteed to support passthrough colorspaces, mainly the proprietary nvidia ones see: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/102987#issuecomment-3554625757 . Since selecting a colorspace which isn't supported will raise errors we need the fallback. It's fine though since because the colorspace is externally managed, the compositor knows what the colorspace actually is (ie not nonlinear sRGB).

Only drivers which make use of the protocol to indicate the colorspace to the compositor support the pass through colorspace. If pass through is not supported we can assume the driver doesn't use the protocol to override what we said our colorspace is and won't cause any issues with double reporting.

If we only enabled externally managing the colorspace when we enable HDR we would need to trust that the vulkan drivers destroy their own color management surface when we switch from an explicit nonlinear sRGB colorspace to 16-bit float passthrough (so that only one surface exists at a time). Even if that may be true, I'm not confident on when they would destroy the surface and is likely to lead to races where we need to guess when it becomes safe to begin managing the surface. The safer option is to always manage the colorspace since in that case there is never a risk that the driver may create it's own management surface.

Also, Allen specifically requested that we unset the color profile of our surfaces when performing SDR, if we disabled externally managing the colorspace when rendering in SDR mesa vulkan drivers would assign some particular colorspace which we do not control. It would also make eventually using the upcoming inverse piece wise sRGB tf more noisy since we would need to add support for managing the colorspace in SDR again.

yes, it's destroyed server-side, but there's still a local proxy you have to take care of. See https://ppaalanen.blogspot.com/2014/07/wayland-protocol-design-object-lifespan.html

> How protocol objects are destroyed
> There are two ways to destroy a protocol object. By far the most common one is to have a request in the interface that is specified to be a destructor. Most often this request is called "destroy". When the client code calls the function wl_foobar_destroy(), the request is sent to the server and the client side proxy (struct wl_proxy) for the object gets destroyed. The server then handles the destructor request at some point in the future.
>
> The other way is to destroy the object by an event. In that case, no destructor must be defined in the interface's protocol specification, and the event must be clearly documented to be destructive as there is no automation nor safeties for this. This is for cases where the server decides when an object dies, and requires extreme care in protocol design to work right in all cases. **When a client receives such an event, all it can do is destroy the proxy. The (in)famous example of an interface like this is wl_callback.**

(Emphasis mine)
I see, I was looking for an explicit destroy method in the protocol, but seems like there was an autogenerated method which calls `wl_proxy_destroy`. Applied comment.

> In theory we could query the rendering context to ask for the colorspace, but that's only updated the frame after we attempt to set HDR and I don't know if there's any loop in the display server which is synced with frames.

`process_events` is a direct part of OS run loop, always called right before `Main::iteration`:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/bf95b62586e31b8a3503f5903d7764d7c52bf2ab/platform/linuxbsd/os_linuxbsd.cpp#L986-L998

Now, as far as I understand it this means that, as long as low consumption mode is *not* enabled, you *will* get a frame after `process_events` (and thus an eventual `wl_surface.commit`).

If low consumption mode is enabled you will need to check for `RenderingServer::get_singleton()->has_changed()`. Then you know that it will render a frame.

This is how I handled frame throttling ("vsync emulation"), see the relevant `DisplayServerWayland` code:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/bf95b62586e31b8a3503f5903d7764d7c52bf2ab/platform/linuxbsd/wayland/display_server_wayland.cpp#L1870-L1894

From RocketChat:

> llmvpipe doesn't support 16-bit floats which is the only (driver) requirement we had for performing HDR on wayland. llvmpipe does however support 16-bit ints which have more banding than floats but otherwise work fine.
>It's as simple as whether we want to allow 16-bit ints or not since I added different logic for detecting if enabling HDR failed (ie if we remove llvmpipe support, someone testing llvmpipe with HDR could attempt to enable HDR, see 1 frame of a washed out scene and then see the scene return to SDR rendering).

I think to have a strong opinion on whether we should support HDR via llvmpipe with 16 bit int buffers I would need to try this out myself first to see how bad the banding is. There is a risk that if we support 16 bit int buffers for HDR (at all, in any scenario) that it will be a worse experience for some users than just falling back to SDR (which would not exhibit banding), and this would be considered a bug in those cases.

So if anyone wants this feature you can hold out until I have time to really test this thoroughly, but the safe thing to do might be to simply fall back to SDR instead of supporting HDR with 16 bit int buffers. Also of relevance: it will be easy to add support for HDR 16 bit int buffers in a future update to Godot, but it will be much more difficult to remove existing support for HDR 16 bit int buffers in Godot if users find that this mode is problematic due to banding and they would instead prefer to simply fall back to SDR.

The litmus test here is: "is banding worse with 8-bit SDR or with HDR 16-bit int and a 200 nits reference luminance?". If there is less banding with 8-bit SDR, then SDR is the "higher quality format" and HDR 16-bit int should never be supported because it is a lower quality format than 8-bit SDR.

During testing, @mahkoh experienced a random crash when testing SDR. I asked and they seemed to be using open-source (mesa) nvidia driver so I concluded that the nvidia mesa driver required us to use `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` to disable color management, even when using SDR.

This matters even though we clear the image format because we create an object (`wp_color_management_surface`) when a window is created. This is the object we use to clear the image and only one can exist per window (creating more than 1 is a protocol error, mainly so that situations like this don't become race conditions). If we allow the driver to color manage in SDR, once we change to HDR, we would need to trust the driver to destroy this object and also need to take a guess as to when it does so to not trigger protocol errors. Instead of trying to guess when it's safe to create a `wp_color_management_surface` I decided to never allow the driver to create one which is why this was needed.

> the heuristic is changed to be whether the compositor is requesting an HDR colorspace for the window

You're checking for gamma22, which KWin *always* requests (since Plasma 6.6), no matter what. A display may also have exact sRGB primaries and still support HDR just fine, and similarly most displays don't have exactly sRGB primaries and don't do HDR. A compositor may also request BT1886 or linear, which both would be interpreted as requesting HDR this way.

Max + reference luminance is the only way you can check for "HDR" being requested.

OK, can we get the same safety by placing these as a lower priority than `VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR`? (Said differently: move this code to be after `VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR` is pushed to the `preferred_formats`)?

The reason I ask is because this would allow us to maintain the existing behaviour in Godot of always using `VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR` for SDR when possible and only falling back to `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` when it is not available.

Specifically, that at 100% brightness HDR is disabled and we return to SDR. Would the frame look different if we can be sure that glare compensation happened? I'm not familiar enough with how the `output_max_value` parameter affects tonemapping but would it be acceptable?

We can't because the formats are placed in order of preference. Since the open source driver supports SDR rendering `VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR` would always be selected.

Now, since the goal is removing `get_colorspace_externally_managed` I asked about what consequences this has for X11.

> Or is switching between SDR and HDR based on the screen brightness the intended behaviour when a user wants to map the full dynamic range of their screen to their Display Configuration brightness slider?

If the user configures the display so `reference == max luminance`, there's no HDR headroom anymore, so it is intended in a way. In an ideal world, applications would present nearly the same image with `reference == 0.99 * max` as with `reference == max`, but of course it's not always that simple.

I assume the reason you don't want to always use the "HDR mode" in rendering is that it's noticeably more expensive in terms of compute?

> Do you happen to know if the issue of apps needing to switch between SDR and HDR mode based on screen brightness is discussed anywhere?

It came up before in the context of browsers needing to decide in advance whether or not they should load the SDR or HDR version of a video, as they can't realistically switch between them once the video has started playing.

Afaik Firefox atm checks the luminance values of all screens for this to know whether or not HDR might be useful, but we considered adding some protocol bit for a HDR video streaming preference - so compositors could prevent HDR video streaming while on battery for example. Maybe something in that direction (but more general) is needed.

> I assume the reason you don't want to always use the "HDR mode" in rendering is that it's noticeably more expensive in terms of compute?

Yes, performance and memory usage is one reason that we do not want Godot games to be operating in HDR mode when the game window is on a screen that does not support HDR output.

For clarity, the goal is not to remove `get_colorspace_externally_managed`. The goal is to move `get_colorspace_externally_managed` out of rendering context driver where it doesn't belong and possibly simplify the code, since this flag simply represents `WAYLAND_ENABLED && wayland_thread.supports_hdr()`.

Now that I understand this better, I'm fine with the logic of `PASS_THROUGH_EXT` being added in this order. I don't like that we're changing the SDR color space used for Wayland games in an HDR PR, but it seems that's the only way to make this work.

From what was said in [this comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/102987#issuecomment-4033102677), it looks like it's fine to have this change for X11, but if there's some way to easily determine `WAYLAND_ENABLED && wayland_thread.supports_hdr()` without needing to add something to the rendering context driver, that would be a good option.

> If the user configures the display so `reference == max luminance`, there's no HDR headroom anymore, so it is intended in a way.

Sounds like this is the way things are designed, so I'm fine with keeping things as they were with `wd.color_profile.target_max_luminance > wd.color_profile.reference_luminance` being the way to determine if it's HDR or not. Sucks for users and players who set their reference luminance and max luminance to be equal and then use their brightness adjustment to control reference luminance, but if there's no way to do this better, then that's outside of our control.

It's best to change this back to the way it was: use `context_driver->get_colorspace_externally_managed()` instead of `#ifdef WAYLAND_ENABLED`.
